On a radiant autumn afternoon in September 1901, President William McKinley stood inside the Temple of Music at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, smiling warmly as he shook hands with thousands of admiring citizens. In line stood Leon Czolgosz, a twenty-eight-year-old Polish-American anarchist whose right hand was wrapped in a white handkerchief concealing a .32-caliber Iver Johnson revolver. Two point-blank gunshots shattered the peaceful afternoon. Yet even as blood poured from his abdomen, McKinley's first thought was of others: 'Be careful how you tell my wife,' he whispered, and urged bystanders not to hurt his assassin. Discover the heartbreaking eight-day battle for McKinley's life, the medical failures in the City of Light, and the midnight horseback dash that made Theodore Roosevelt president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of William McKinley with one of the most fateful turning points in the history of the American presidency. At the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, a city illuminated by the electrical wonder of Niagara Falls, an assassin's bullet ended the life of a gentle, beloved leader and thrust thirty-six-year-old Theodore Roosevelt into the White House. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CITY OF LIGHT AND ELECTRIC WONDER
In the late summer of 1901, the city of Buffalo, New York, was the center of the technological world. The Pan-American Exposition had transformed three hundred and fifty acres into an architectural dreamscape nicknamed the 'Rainbow City.' The exposition celebrated the dawn of the electrical age, powered by the colossal hydroelectric generators newly installed at Niagara Falls. Every evening at dusk, over one hundred thousand incandescent light bulbs illuminated the massive Electric Tower, casting a golden, fairy-tale glow across the canals and plazas.\n\nOn September 4, President William McKinley arrived in Buffalo aboard the presidential train, accompanied by his beloved, epileptic wife Ida. The following day, over one hundred thousand spectators packed the exposition grounds to hear McKinley deliver what would be his final public address. In a visionary speech that surprised many of his conservative supporters, McKinley urged the nation to look beyond protectionism toward reciprocal international trade: 'Isolation is no longer possible or desirable,' McKinley declared. 'God and man have linked the nations together. The period of exclusiveness is past. The expansion of our trade and commerce is the pressing problem. Commercial wars are unprofitable. A policy of goodwill and friendly trade relations will prevent reprisals.' It was a magnificent, progressive roadmap for twentieth-century global leadership.\n\nThe Pan-American Exposition's dazzling electrical displays symbolized the limitless promise of American technological genius at the dawn of the twentieth century. Millions of incandescent bulbs reflected across the grand basins, mesmerizing crowds from across the globe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ANARCHIST IN THE SHADOWS
Listening intently in the dense crowd was twenty-eight-year-old Leon Frank Czolgosz. Born in Michigan to poor Polish immigrant parents, Czolgosz had worked from childhood in wire mills and glass factories in Cleveland and Chicago. Shaken by the brutal suppression of the Pullman Strike and radicalized by the fiery speeches of anarchist Emma Goldman, Czolgosz came to believe that the American capitalist system was an evil conspiracy that enslaved working people. In 1900, Italian anarchist Gaetano Bresci had assassinated King Umberto I of Italy, sparking a wave of anarchist terrorism across Europe.\n\nCzolgosz became convinced that it was his sacred duty as an anarchist to strike down the head of the American government: 'I thought it would be a good thing for them to know that an American could kill a ruler,' he later confessed. On September 3, Czolgosz bought a small, concealable .32-caliber Iver Johnson revolver for four dollars and fifty cents at a Buffalo hardware store. For two days, he stalked McKinley through the exposition grounds, waiting for an opportunity to get close to the President.\n\nCzolgosz's ideological radicalization reflected the deep social fractures and violent industrial conflicts that accompanied America's rapid transformation into an industrial titan. He drifted between boarding houses and radical gatherings, nursing delusions of revolutionary vengeance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FATEFUL HANDSHAKE AT THE TEMPLE OF MUSIC
Friday, September 6, 1901, was sweltering and humid. McKinley spent the morning visiting Niagara Falls, returning to the exposition grounds in the afternoon for a public reception in the Temple of Music. McKinley loved greeting the public; he was a master of the 'McKinley handshake'—a swift, gentle grasp that guided visitors along before they could squeeze his hand. His personal secretary, George B. Cortelyou, was terrified of an assassination attempt and had twice removed the reception from the official schedule, but McKinley insisted on meeting the people: 'Why should I be afraid?' McKinley told him. 'No one would wish to hurt me.'\n\nAt four o'clock, the pipe organ began playing Schumann's 'Traumerei' as thousands of citizens filed into the auditorium. The line moved rapidly past the President, who was flanked by three Secret Service agents, municipal detectives, and a detachment of soldiers. Around 4:07 PM, Leon Czolgosz stepped forward. His right hand was wrapped in a clean white linen handkerchief, making it appear that he was nursing an injured hand. Secret Service agents noticed the bandage, but assuming it was harmless, allowed him to pass. When McKinley smiled and extended his hand in friendship, Czolgosz slapped the President's hand away, shoved the concealed revolver against McKinley's abdomen, and fired twice through the handkerchief.\n\nMcKinley's determination to greet ordinary citizens in the Temple of Music demonstrated his enduring democratic faith that an American president belonged among the people. He believed that building barriers between the chief executive and the citizens was fundamentally un-American.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 'DON'T LET THEM HURT HIM'
The two gunshots sounded like firecrackers above the pipe organ. Smoke billowed from the burning linen handkerchief. The first bullet struck a brass button on McKinley's waistcoat, deflecting harmlessly into the fabric of his coat. But the second bullet tore directly into the President's abdomen, penetrating both the front and rear walls of his stomach, grazing a kidney, and embedding deep in the muscles of his back. McKinley staggered backward into the arms of his secretary, blood staining his white vest.\n\nInstantly, total pandemonium erupted. A towering African American waiter named James Parker, who was standing directly behind Czolgosz in line, lunged forward with a ferocious right hook, striking the assassin in the face and knocking the revolver from his hand. Detectives and soldiers piled onto Czolgosz, beating him mercilessly with gun butts and fists. Through his agonizing pain, William McKinley demonstrated the extraordinary, saintly grace that defined his character. Seeing the soldiers beating the assassin on the floor, McKinley whispered faintly: 'Don't let them hurt him.' Then, turning to his weeping secretary, McKinley thought only of his invalid wife: 'My wife—be careful, Cortelyou, how you tell her. Oh, be careful.'\n\nEven in the shock of a fatal wound, McKinley's instinctive concern for his wife and his compassion for his assailant revealed the saintly gentleness of his character. Those who witnessed his calm whispered words wept at the sight of such unselfish nobility.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FLAWED SURGERY IN THE EXPOSITION HOSPITAL
McKinley was rushed in an electric ambulance to the small, rudimentary exposition hospital. The top surgeon in Buffalo, Dr. Roswell Park, was fifty miles away in Niagara Falls performing a delicate cancer operation. In his absence, the emergency surgery was taken over by Dr. Matthew D. Mann, a prominent gynecological surgeon who had rarely operated on gunshot wounds. As the afternoon light faded, Mann operated on McKinley on an ordinary wooden table, using reflected sunlight bounced off a handheld mirror because the hospital had no electric overhead surgical lamps.\n\nMann successfully sutured the entry and exit holes in the President's stomach, but could not locate the bullet buried deep in his back. Fearing that further probing would cause lethal hemorrhaging, Mann closed the incision without inserting a surgical drainage tube—a fatal medical mistake. In the days that followed, the nation held its breath. McKinley appeared to recover with astonishing speed; his fever dropped, he joked with doctors, and on September 10, he was permitted to drink beef broth and eat solid food. Reassured by optimistic medical bulletins, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt left Buffalo and took his family on a camping vacation in the high peaks of the Adirondack Mountains.\n\nThe lack of electrical lighting in the hospital and the failure to install surgical drainage tubes highlighted the tragic limitations of emergency medicine at the turn of the century. Doctors relied on optimistic exterior signs while toxic sepsis advanced silently beneath the sutures.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SUDDEN TURN AND 'NEARER, MY GOD, TO THEE'
The optimism was a lethal illusion. Because no drainage tube had been installed, gangrene and systemic sepsis had taken root deep inside the abdominal cavity. On Thursday, September 12, McKinley's pulse soared to an alarming one hundred and thirty beats a minute. His digestive system shut down, his kidneys failed, and his heart began to give out under the toxic shock of blood poisoning. Urgent telegrams were dispatched across the nation: the President was sinking fast.\n\nOn Friday evening, September 13, McKinley regained consciousness and realized that his end was near. He asked for his frail wife Ida to be brought to his bedside. Taking her trembling hand in his, McKinley whispered softly: 'Goodbye, goodbye all. It is God's way. His will, not ours, be done.' He began quietly humming his favorite hymn, 'Nearer, My God, to Thee.' At 2:15 on the morning of Saturday, September 14, 1901, President William McKinley breathed his last. He was fifty-eight years old. Across the nation, church bells tolled, and millions of citizens wept openly in the streets for the gentle gentleman from Ohio.\n\nMcKinley's peaceful acceptance of death and his whispered prayers comforted a grief-stricken nation, uniting citizens across all political and regional divides. His Christian fortitude in his final hours became a lasting symbol of nineteenth-century American piety.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MIDNIGHT DASH OF THEODORE ROOSEVELT
Deep in the wilderness of the Adirondack Mountains, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt had just climbed the summit of Mount Marcy when a trail guide brought him a breathless message: McKinley was dying. Roosevelt raced down the mountain on foot, boarded a buckboard wagon, and began a harrowing midnight dash across pitch-black mountain roads, changing exhausted horses three times at remote relay stations as lanterns swung over rocky cliffs. At dawn on September 14, Roosevelt reached the railroad station at North Creek, where he received the telegraph informing him that William McKinley was dead.\n\nRoosevelt boarded a special locomotive that raced at seventy miles an hour to Buffalo. At 3:30 that afternoon, in the library of the Wilcox mansion on Delaware Avenue, forty-two-year-old Theodore Roosevelt raised his right hand and took the presidential oath, becoming the youngest President in the history of the United States. Leon Czolgosz was swiftly tried, convicted, and executed in the electric chair at Auburn Prison forty-five days later. The gentle Gilded Age era of consensus politics, gold standards, and dignified front porches was buried alongside William McKinley. In its place stepped the kinetic, crusading energy of Theodore Roosevelt, and the Progressive Era had begun.\n\nThe assassination of William McKinley ended the Gilded Age and propelled the kinetic, reforming spirit of Theodore Roosevelt onto the world stage. An era of dignified restraint gave way to the bold, crusading vigor of the modern American Century.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
William McKinley's tragic death marked the end of an era and the dramatic birth of modern American presidential power. His personal grace in the face of death remained an inspiration to a grieving nation. Next week, we begin our portrait of the man who took his place—Theodore Roosevelt—the dynamic whirlwind who stormed into the White House, settled the Coal Strike of 1902, busted the railroad trusts, and built the Panama Canal. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
